title: The forest dwellers
hookLine: who were the old people living in the forest, and why had they gone there at all?
last: THE CROWN GOES. THE DUTY STAYS.

cards: Take a retired couple: the kids are grown, there are grandchildren, the house is paid off. Today they might downsize, or travel. The old law books describe another option: go to the forest.
Leave the house to your children, take a few things, and spend the rest of your life on prayer and simple living. Some readers picture the people who greeted Rama in that ring of huts this way.

teach.b: Hindu law books describe life in four stages, called ashramas. First the student, learning. Then the householder, raising a family and working.
Third, vanaprastha, literally the forest dweller. The Laws of Manu say a householder may take this step when he sees his skin wrinkled, his hair gray, and his children's children born.
He can go with his wife or alone, eat what grows wild, keep the sacred fires and study. For some, a fourth stage: complete renunciation. It was an ideal, and not everyone lived it, then or now.
But it gave the forest a shape. Not only wilderness: a place people went to finish their lives well. Among them were the great sages.
Two words come up again and again.
A rishi is a seer, one to whom sacred hymns were revealed. A muni is often explained as the silent one, whose practice includes holding back speech. What they share is tapas.

The word means heat, and it's used for the discipline of austerity: fasting, standing in the sun, sitting through the cold. In the epics, tapas builds real power; a sage's blessing or curse can change a king's fate.
That makes their request to Rama more striking. They aren't helpless. They've chosen not to fight.

teach.h: DRESSED LIKE THEM, WITH A BOW.
teach.b: And here comes Rama, dressed just like them in bark and matted hair, but carrying a bow.

how: The four stages of life remain an ideal in Hindu teaching; some older Hindus today take on a simpler, more prayerful life after their working years, though few literally move to the forest.

forest seers and ascetics who live by tapas and choose not to fight

p: the forest dweller, the third stage

s: Hindu law books describe four stages of life
the forest sages are powerless, so they need Rama
in the epics their tapas gives real power; they've chosen not to fight.
a forest dweller could go with his wife
the Laws of Manu allow him to go with her or alone.

games.q: you're a householder in the world of the old law books. your hair is gray and your grandchildren are born. what do the books describe next?
o: go to the forest as a vanaprastha.
games.why: the Laws of Manu describe this as the time to leave for the forest, with your wife or alone.

practice: Try a small taste of the muni's practice: silence, not even words in your head if you can help it. When a list or a reply starts up inside, let it trail off unfinished, and come back to the sound of your breathing.

wordCard.voice: The sages. Forest dwellers, seers and silent ones, living by tapas, the heat of discipline, who chose not to fight.

orig.note: Sanskrit tapas: heat, glow; used for austerity, the discipline that, in the epics, gives sages power.

carryVoice: Your line: tapas, the heat of discipline. The quietest people in the forest are far from powerless. Day five hundred fifty-one, done.
